text:
Project Polaris just changed what's running your Copilot.

Microsoft swapped GPT-4 Turbo for its own in-house coding model as Copilot's new default engine — same interface, different brain underneath.

What it actually does: routes your coding requests through Microsoft's own model, tuned across languages, with the old model still available as a fallback for now.

Why builders should care: your tools are getting smarter and more opinionated at the same time. The stack under "Copilot" isn't fixed — it's a choice, and knowing what's running matters as much as knowing how to prompt it.

Try this: open your Copilot settings this week and check which model is actually answering you. Test the same prompt against two models and compare.

The signal: AI tools are moving from "one vendor, one model" to a mixture of engines under one roof. Fluency now includes knowing what's under the hood.

text:
Stop running one AI chat. Build an org chart instead.

On Tech Thursday we talked about treating AI like a team, not a single conversation — sub-agents that each own a role and run in parallel.

Here's the shape we use: a chief of staff to hold the plan, a project manager to sequence the work, a technical architect to design it, a tester to catch what breaks, and a marketing/social/UX layer to ship it.

One prompt becomes a fanned-out workflow. You review the plan, agents execute, you approve the output. That's the whole loop.

This content engine runs on exactly this pattern — built entirely on GitHub Copilot CLI.

Comment BUILD and I'll send you the workflow map.
